name: Pacific Northwest Rainforest
blurb: Giant conifers, mossy elk country and salmon that feed the forest from the sea.

sources.title: Helfield & Naiman 2001, Ecology: salmon-derived nitrogen and riparian forest growth

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Hoh Rainforest, Olympic National Park, Temperate rainforest). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Gaps in the tall canopy let light reach the mosses, shrubs and seedlings below.
A giant conifer of the wet coastal forest. Near spawning streams its foliage draws a share of its nitrogen from salmon carcasses.
One of the main canopy conifers of the Olympic rainforest, alongside spruce and Douglas-fir.
A tall canopy conifer; old stands of it provide the nesting habitat northern spotted owls need.
A large yellow forest slug that eats fungi, plant matter and litter, and helps spread seeds.
Omnivore that eats berries, shoots and insects, and fishes for salmon in the Pacific coast; it also strips bark.
In the Pacific Northwest, spawning salmon make up most of its diet from late summer through fall, mostly scavenged carcasses.
The park's top land predator; deer and elk are the main prey of cougars, and it is among the predators of elk.

link_ideas.what: Salmon carry marine nitrogen from the ocean into forest streams

story: Olympic's Hoh Rainforest is among the rainiest places in the United States. Sitka spruce and western hemlock here can top 90 m, and mosses coat their bark. Salmon feed on ocean krill, then black bears and bald eagles feed on the salmon. Cougars hunt elk.
matters: Olympic National Park is a World Heritage Site and a biosphere reserve. Inside it the forest is protected from commercial exploitation, but much of the forest along the river below the park was logged within the last century.
